EU–UK summit: a leaked draft declaration shows a real but limited rapprochement, ahead of Andy Burnham's visit to Brussels on Friday

On Wednesday 18 November, Euronews revealed the draft declaration for the EU–UK summit scheduled for Friday 20 November in Brussels. Youth mobility, the carbon market, food: the text makes progress, but access to the single market remains closed and several points have been dropped [1][2][3].
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham is due to travel to Brussels on Friday to conclude agreements on food and drink, youth mobility and access to the European carbon market [3].

On students, the draft leaves two options: the same tuition fees for Europeans as for British students, or significantly reduced undergraduate fees [1]. This sensitive issue has been deferred to a separate agreement [1]. According to Euronews, the EU is demanding at least 100,000 young people for the scheme [1].

The two sides are expected to confirm the linking of their emissions trading systems, the markets where industrial companies pay to pollute, but without a start date [1]. The UK's entry into the European electricity market is still blocked [1].

The text promises a lasting solution for British steel shipped to Northern Ireland [1]. However, it drops the European demand to suspend the British scheme for deporting convicted foreign nationals, and a reference to coordinating state aid and public procurement has disappeared [1].
According to a source quoted by The Independent, the talks are going "down to the wire"; London is reluctant to sign with the Commission on matters that fall under the member states [3].
Brussels warns that once these agreements are signed, there will be no more "à la carte" access to parts of the single market for the United Kingdom [2].

Key takeaway: London and Brussels are moving closer sector by sector, but the EU refuses to let the United Kingdom pick and choose what suits it. Going further would mean joining the single market, and therefore accepting its rules [2].

The stakes are concrete: a shared carbon market, easier food trade and simpler stays for young people are the three agreements London wants to sign on Friday [3]. But no date has been set for linking the carbon markets, and electricity remains blocked [1]. Youth mobility remains the most sensitive issue in the United Kingdom, where opponents see it as a risk of uncontrolled immigration [3].
According to commentators quoted by The Independent, Andy Burnham could present broader options for the relationship with the EU in December [3].

If you are a student or a young worker, this summit could reopen the door to studying or working in the United Kingdom at a lower cost. For French exporters of wine, cheese or fresh produce, a food agreement would reduce border checks.

news.2026-11-19-apec-trump-ia-regulation: AI: at APEC in China, Trump rejects any global rules on "superintelligence", while Xi Jinping calls for an "open ecosystem"

On Thursday 19 November in Shenzhen, before the leaders gathered at the APEC summit, Donald Trump rejected any "globalist regulation" of artificial intelligence, which he calls "superintelligence". His host Xi Jinping, by contrast, called for an "open ecosystem" for AI and promised to lower Chinese tariffs [1][2][4][5].

At the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting, Trump declared: "We oppose any form of globalist regulation or anything that would seek to control or stifle superintelligence, and we will not let that happen" [1][2][8].

He presented the United States as the world leader in this technology, which he sees as the biggest upheaval since the Industrial Revolution [2]. He did, however, acknowledge risks: "We have to be very careful in managing these downsides" [3].
Trump also touted the US economy and offered American gas to Asia, citing an approved pipeline in Alaska to deliver it to the region [1].

Xi Jinping described AI as one of the "engines of innovation-driven growth" and asked members to "build an open ecosystem" [4]. "Starting with lowering tariffs and expanding market access, China will carry out in-depth reforms," he promised [5].
The day before, speaking to business leaders gathered in Shenzhen, Xi had called for "deepening cooperation in the digital economy and AI" [6].
Trump's speech comes four days after the "San Francisco Declaration", signed on 15 November by the United States and nine partner countries, including India [2].

Key takeaway: on AI, the world's two leading powers are defending opposing visions. Washington rejects any international rules that could hold back its companies; Beijing presents itself as a champion of open cooperation, while it faces the threat of new US restrictions on access to advanced AI chips [1][4][7].

Trump has long rejected any formal regulation of the most powerful AI models, considering US laws sufficient [2]. In 2025, at the APEC summit in South Korea, which Trump did not attend, Xi had proposed a World AI Cooperation Organization to set its rules [2].

Common ground remains possible on safety: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced that the two countries would discuss at APEC protocols for alerting each other in the event of an AI-related incident and exchanges on how to test advanced models [7].
These speeches serve as a prelude to Thursday's three-way summit between Trump, Xi and Vladimir Putin, where trade and technology carry a lot of weight [1][7].

Washington's refusal of any global rules means that the AI you use every day, often American, will remain regulated mainly country by country, for example by Europe. And the US-China rivalry over AI weighs on the price and availability of chips, and therefore on your phones and computers.

Japan-China: in Shenzhen, Takaichi talks, Xi smiles without a word, and Washington's Asian allies tread on eggshells

On Wednesday 18 and Thursday 19 November, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi shook hands twice with Xi Jinping at the APEC summit in Shenzhen, their first contact since relations froze a year ago. Xi responded only with a smile. Australia and South Korea, for their part, are awaiting their one-on-one meetings [1][2][5][6].

At the APEC welcome dinner on Wednesday evening, Sanae Takaichi said a few words to Xi Jinping after their handshake; the Chinese president responded only with a smile, according to the South China Morning Post [1].
It was their first in-person exchange since last autumn, when relations froze after Takaichi's remarks on Taiwan [1].
On Thursday, the two leaders shook hands again, for the second day in a row; Takaichi appeared to speak to Xi for a moment, though what was said is not known [2][3].

Chinese protocol sent a signal: at Shenzhen airport, Takaichi was greeted by a former Chinese Foreign Ministry official rather than a serving one, whereas other leaders received more courtesy [1]. No one-on-one meeting has been announced [1].

Australia's Anthony Albanese is due to meet Xi on Friday, for their fifth official meeting, with representatives of mining giants BHP and Rio Tinto in his delegation [4][5]. "The relationship with China is solid," he says [4][5].
South Korea wants to use its summit with Xi to continue the "full restoration" of relations, as agreed by foreign ministers Cho Hyun and Wang Yi on 13 November in Beijing [6].
Key takeaway: China calibrates its gestures country by country. Japan, which spoke out on Taiwan, is kept at arm's length, while other US allies get real meetings [1][4][6].

The context makes things harder for Beijing's neighbours: Donald Trump has announced joint military exercises with his Quad partners, Australia, India and Japan, which could displease China [5][7]. Albanese says he does not fear Chinese retaliation [7].
Australia also has a direct trade interest: asked about China's central iron ore purchasing agency, Foreign Minister Penny Wong only said that negotiations are under way [4][5].

Seoul, for its part, is counting on Beijing to revive dialogue with North Korea; this would be the third summit between Lee Jae-myung and Xi Jinping, after APEC in Gyeongju in 2025 and Lee's state visit to Beijing in January [6].

Japan, Australia and South Korea are key suppliers of cars, electronics, minerals and chips. When their relations with China become tense or warm up, it affects global supply chains, and therefore the prices of the products you buy.

Colombia: unions and teachers on national strike this Thursday against Abelardo de la Espriella's fiscal "rescue law", despite his U-turn on VAT

This Thursday, 19 November, the CUT trade union federation, the Fecode teachers' union and pensioners' organisations are calling a 24-hour national strike against President Abelardo de la Espriella's "economic rescue law". The movement is going ahead despite the announced withdrawal of VAT on basic food products [1][2][3].

The CUT called the day of action together with the Comando Nacional Unitario of labour federations, pensioners' confederations and other social sectors [3]. According to Bloomberg Línea, Fecode confirmed its participation in this 24-hour strike, which may disrupt classes in public schools [1].
The targeted bill, the "economic rescue law", was submitted to Congress on Thursday 29 October [4]. The government wants it to raise revenue in the face of the difficult state of public finances [5].

On Sunday 15 November, the president announced that he would withdraw the articles that subjected certain basic food basket products to VAT [2][5]. Fecode nevertheless maintained its call, issued as early as 9 November in a circular [2].

The unions also denounce the increase in health contributions, while corporate income tax would fall from 35% to 31% [5][3]. CUT leader Fabio Arias calls it a "regressive" reform, meaning one that weighs more heavily on low-income households [4].

On the other side, the Finance Ministry highlights a VAT refund that would reach 19 million people [4]. Former left-wing president Gustavo Petro argues that removing the tax on food does not prevent the rising cost of living for households [5].

The organisers are targeting "the fascist government of Abelardo de la Espriella and its tax reform", according to their call quoted by Colombia Reports [6]. The Historic Pact, the left-wing coalition, has also confirmed a national mobilisation [7].
In Bogotá, street closures and disruptions on the TransMilenio bus network are expected, with gathering points throughout the city [8][9].

Key takeaway: this is the first major street test for Abelardo de la Espriella, the right-wing president who took office on 7 August [4]. His U-turn on VAT on food was not enough to defuse the unions' anger [5][2].

Nothing is settled yet: the bill must be debated in the Senate and then in the House of Representatives [2]. The scale of Thursday's mobilisation will weigh on lawmakers, who can still amend the text.

The protest goes beyond the budget alone. Fecode adds its own demands on teachers' careers and rejects other bills on public education [2][1]. The unions are also highlighting health and labour issues [2].

Colombia exports a lot of coffee, flowers and oil to Europe: prolonged protests could disrupt this trade. If you are travelling in the country this Thursday, expect disrupted transport in the major cities, starting with Bogotá.

Brazil: the Senate wraps up Lula's savings plan by 69 votes to 2, with the Chamber of Deputies convened as early as Monday

On Wednesday 18 November, the Brazilian Senate completed its vote on the Lula government's fiscal adjustment plan, intended to improve the public accounts by 45 to 56 billion reais in 2027. Passed by 69 votes to 2, the bill now goes to the Chamber of Deputies, convened for an extraordinary session on Monday 23 November [1][2][3][4].
The base text had been approved on Thursday 12 November by 45 votes to 31; four opposition amendments remained to be decided [5][6]. Three were rejected and one withdrawn after an agreement [6].

The toughest amendment, from opposition senator Rogério Marinho, sought to limit spending growth to 0.6% above inflation instead of 2%; it was rejected by 47 votes to 30 [2][6]. The text was then approved by 69 votes to 2, with one abstention [2].

To unblock the vote, rapporteur Eduardo Braga (MDB) agreed to ease the schedule of compensation payments that the federal government makes to states and municipalities under the Kandir Law [6][1]. According to Tribuna do Sertão, the annual amount rises from 1 to 2 billion reais [6].

At the heart of the plan: from 2027, in years when austerity measures are taken, federal spending will not be allowed to grow by more than 2% above inflation, compared with 2.5% today [7][3]. The government will also be able to freeze additional spending to meet its target [7].

Senators kept the measure allowing limits on companies' use of their tax credits to pay federal taxes, one of the plan's main sources of revenue [6]. The text also provides for a cut of about 10% in tax breaks, or some 15 billion reais in revenue in 2027 [8].

The government estimates the gain at between 45.1 and 56.1 billion reais for the 2027 primary balance, meaning the budget excluding interest on the debt [3]. CartaCapital mentions up to 60 billion [4]. The Speaker of the Chamber, Hugo Motta, announced an extraordinary session on Monday 23 November [4].

Key takeaway: this plan is meant to show that Brazil keeps its accounts in order, and its adoption is a precondition for the 2027 budget, whose vote is scheduled for 17 December [6]. The government is therefore in a hurry [6].

Lula's camp emphasises spending control without cuts to social programmes [9]. The opposition wanted a much tougher brake, with spending growth limited to 0.6% above inflation, but it was defeated [2].

The text also excludes up to 10.5 billion reais of diesel subsidies in 2026 from the calculation of the fiscal target [7]. An exception that shows how hard it is to meet the target when energy is expensive.
In the Chamber, the rapporteur has already said he wants to keep the Senate's version, which could speed up final adoption [10].

Brazil is a Latin American giant and a major supplier of raw materials to Europe. Better-managed public finances should, in principle, mean a more stable real: if you have an "emerging markets" fund in your savings, Brazil is part of it.

Egypt: the IMF agrees to pay out a final $2.3bn, and Cairo then wants to do without it

On Wednesday 18 November, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) reached an agreement with Egypt on the final review of its assistance programme. If approved by its board before 15 December, Cairo will receive about $2.3bn, bringing the total disbursed to about $9.6bn [1][2].

The so-called "staff-level" agreement was reached between IMF staff and the Egyptian government: it concludes the eighth and final review of the $8bn loan granted under the "Extended Fund Facility" [2][3].

It provides for about $1.5bn under this loan and up to $0.8bn under a second fund, the "Resilience and Sustainability Facility" [2][5]. No money will be disbursed before approval by the IMF Executive Board [3].
Amine Mati's mission negotiated in Cairo from 25 October to 5 November, left without an agreement, and talks then continued by videoconference until 15 November [2][4].

"Successful implementation of the reform programme and a proactive response to the consequences of the war in the Middle East have helped preserve stability," said Amine Mati [2]. According to him, Egypt exceeded its end-September targets for the budget surplus excluding interest on the debt and for tax revenue [2].

The IMF nevertheless calls for maintaining a flexible exchange rate, which must remain "the first line of defence" against external shocks, and a tight monetary policy to bring inflation down towards the central bank's 7% target [2].

It welcomes the sale of shares in Banque du Caire and the promised acceleration of privatisations [2]. President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi has already announced that Egypt will not request new financing from the IMF and has called for a "national programme" for the period afterwards [1][2].

Key takeaway: Egypt is preparing to exit the IMF assistance programme, which will have disbursed about $9.6bn to it [2]. This final payment should help it get through the end of the year, but the institution warns that high debt and large financing needs remain the main vulnerabilities [2].

In particular, the IMF is asking Cairo to rely less on short-term borrowing, which must be constantly rolled over and becomes expensive when rates rise [1][2]. The government has committed to a primary budget surplus of 5% of GDP for the 2026-2027 fiscal year [2].

The war with Iran has complicated matters: the IMF itself cites the "consequences of the war in the Middle East" among the shocks the country has had to absorb [2]. And the timetable is tight: both arrangements expire on 15 December [2][4].
Leaving the IMF is a gamble: Cairo frees itself from its conditions, but loses a lender of last resort while the region remains at war [1][2].

Egypt is a very popular destination for French holidaymakers: a flexible exchange rate means an Egyptian pound that could fall further, making a stay cheaper for you in euros, but life more expensive for Egyptians. Its stability also matters for the Suez Canal, through which some of the products you buy pass.

Ethiopia-Eritrea: the two armies massed face to face on the border, raising fears of a new war in the Horn of Africa

On Wednesday 18 November, Reuters reported, citing conflict monitors, that Ethiopia and Eritrea have massed troops along their border, within firing range of each other. Drone and artillery strikes have been reported around Badme since 12 November [1][3].

According to the conflict monitor ACLED, the International Crisis Group and two people close to rival Tigrayan militias, the two armies are now within striking distance [1]. Reuters was unable to independently confirm direct clashes between them [1][2].

Accounts differ: a source close to the Tigray Peace Force, allied with the government, says there have been no clashes, while a person linked to the rebels mentions sporadic fighting [1]. Analyst Magnus Taylor of the International Crisis Group does not confirm any clashes, but warns that the situation could escalate [1][3].

According to ACLED, Ethiopian drones struck probable Eritrean positions around Badme on 12 November, and Eritrean artillery retaliated [3]. Residents are fleeing nighttime shelling, according to the outlet Addis Standard [4].
The escalation follows the Ethiopian army's offensive against Tigrayan rebels: it took the town of Sheraro on 3 November and then settled in Adi Awala, on the road to Badme [5].

Eritrea's Information Minister described the accusations by Ethiopia's ruling party as "propaganda", without mentioning the troop movements [1]. Addis Ababa accuses Asmara of sending soldiers to help the Tigrayan rebels, which Eritrea denies [1].
Meeting in Paris, G7 foreign ministers expressed their "deep concern" over the deteriorating security situation [4].

Key takeaway: two countries that have already fought each other could do so again. From 1998 to 2000, their border conflict killed tens of thousands of people [1]. They signed a peace deal in 2018 and fought on the same side during the Tigray civil war from 2020 to 2022 [1].

At the heart of the dispute: the sea. Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed is demanding access to the Red Sea, and Asmara accuses him of wanting to seize the Eritrean port of Assab by force [1]. Abiy replies that he wants to obtain this access by peaceful means [1].

The stakes go beyond the two countries: the Red Sea is one of the major trade routes between Asia and Europe, and the dispute concerns a port on its African shore [1]. The concern expressed by the G7 shows that the major powers are closely watching this new flashpoint [4].
For now, the information relies mainly on diplomatic sources and ACLED, without independent confirmation of who fired on whom: caution is still warranted [1][3].

Some of the products you buy from Asia pass through the Red Sea before the Suez Canal. Another war on this route, already shaken by the conflict with Iran, could further lengthen cargo ships' journeys and weigh on shipping prices.

news.2026-11-19-espagne-debat-sanchez-fe: Spain: ten days before the general election, Sánchez seeks a comeback against Feijóo in the only televised debate, trailing in almost every poll

On Thursday evening, 19 November, Socialist Pedro Sánchez and conservative Alberto Núñez Feijóo face off in the only head-to-head debate of the campaign for the 29 November general election. The People's Party leads in 16 of the 18 polling firms, and could govern with the far-right Vox [1][5][6].
The debate takes place on the set of the Television Academy in Madrid, moderated by journalist María Casado; a draw gave the opening to Feijóo and the closing to Sánchez [1].
